first-americans-founders.description: The ancestors that Ancient Beringians and all other Native Americans share. No one from this population has been sampled; later genomes show it combined East Asian-related ancestry with ancestry related to a Siberian who lived at Mal'ta about 24,000 years ago.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Geneticists call a population like this a ghost population: it is inferred from the shape of the family tree that sampled genomes draw. The clearest evidence comes from two ancient genomes. USR1, from Upward Sun River in Alaska about 11,500 years ago, sits on a branch that split off before all other known Native American lineages separated from one another. Anzick-1, an infant from Montana about 12,600 years old, is more closely related to every Indigenous American population tested than to any other group. The population described here is the shared trunk from which both lines branched.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: Its timeline comes from demographic models, which search for the split dates and mixing events that best reproduce the genetic variation in a set of genomes. Moreno-Mayar and colleagues (2018) date its separation from East Asians to about 36,000 years ago, with gene flow between the two continuing until about 25,000 years ago. Sikora and colleagues (2019) put the split nearer 30,000 years ago, although their uncertainty range of 26,800–36,400 years reaches the earlier figure. Raghavan and colleagues (2015) have the ancestors of all present-day Native Americans entering the Americas from Siberia in a single wave no earlier than 23,000 years ago, after at most about 8,000 years of isolation in Beringia, the lands around the Bering Strait.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Mal'ta-related strand is the smaller of the two. MA-1, who lived in south-central Siberia, was not closely related to East Asians, and Raghavan and colleagues (2014) estimate that ancestry related to him may make up 14–38 percent of Native American ancestry, between about a seventh and two-fifths. A model by Sikora and colleagues that instead uses older Siberian genomes from Yana, the Ancient North Siberians, as the reference finds about 18 percent in the Upward Sun River genome. Anzick-1 already carries this mixture, which is older than the split into northern and southern branches; two models date it to between about 25,000 and 20,000 years ago.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The population later divided, and the dates for that differ too. In Moreno-Mayar and colleagues' model the Ancient Beringian line branched off 22,000–18,100 years ago, and the remaining ancestors split into northern and southern Native American branches 17,500–14,600 years ago; Raghavan and colleagues date the split into two basal branches to about 13,000 years ago. Anzick-1 sits on or near the southern branch, and Central and South Americans radiated rapidly from one of the two. Not every later strand of Indigenous American ancestry traces to this population: later gene flow left some Native Americans sharing ancestry with present-day East Asians.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Where this population lived is not known. Sikora and colleagues' models suggest a refuge across southern Beringia during the coldest part of the last Ice Age; in one scenario they sketch, alongside an alternative, groups related to the Ancient North Siberians met East Asian-related people there, and the Ancient Beringians separated in eastern Beringia. Raghavan and colleagues think the split between the Athabascan and Amerindian lineages more likely happened in lower-latitude North America than in Alaska. Whether one founding population is enough is also debated: Skoglund and colleagues trace an Australasian-related signal in some Amazonian groups to a separate founding source, while Raghavan and colleagues attribute such sharing to later gene flow.

caveats: The timeline shows this population from the modelled split from East Asians to the youngest modelled date for the north–south divergence in Moreno-Mayar et al. 2018, a paper checked against its abstract only; these are model dates, not a record of how long the population existed.

ancient-beringians.description: The earliest-branching line of Native American ancestry sampled so far, known from USR1, an individual from Upward Sun River in Alaska about 11,500 years ago. Its lineage split off before all other known Native American lineages separated from one another.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Two studies place USR1 on the family tree independently. Moreno-Mayar and colleagues (2018) treat the genome as the representative of a distinct population and call it Ancient Beringian, after Beringia, the region around the Bering Strait; Posth and colleagues (2018) reach the same placement in an analysis of their own. The line itself is far older than USR1. In a demographic model by Moreno-Mayar and colleagues, it branched from the shared ancestors of Native Americans 22,000–18,100 years ago, some 6,600–10,500 years before USR1 lived.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: USR1 carries the Siberian-related strand found in Native American ancestry. Sikora and colleagues (2019) estimate that about 18 percent of the genome, nearly a fifth, comes from people related to the Ancient North Siberians known from 31,000-year-old genomes at Yana, and that this ancestry reached the shared ancestors of Ancient Beringians and other Native Americans about 20,000 years ago. Their model runs on a different clock from Moreno-Mayar's, though: it separates those shared ancestors from East Asians about 30,000 years ago, where Moreno-Mayar's has about 36,000.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Where the Ancient Beringian line separated is uncertain. Sikora and colleagues' models point to a refuge across southern Beringia during the coldest part of the last Ice Age, and in one scenario they describe, while offering an alternative, the Ancient Beringians diverged from the ancestors of other Native Americans in eastern Beringia. Raghavan and colleagues favour lower-latitude North America over Alaska for a different, later split, between the Athabascan and Amerindian lineages, so the two studies address different branchings rather than contradicting each other.

caveats: Two individuals from one site, Upward Sun River, are on the map; the findings on this page concern one of them, USR1.
The Moreno-Mayar et al. 2018 findings on this page were checked against the paper's abstract only; USR1's place on the family tree is also supported by Posth et al. 2018, checked in full.

clovis-anzick.description: A baby boy buried with Clovis tools in Montana about 12,600 years ago. His genome is closer to every Indigenous American population tested than to any other group, and the study of it finds no support for the idea that Clovis toolmaking came from Europe.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Anzick-1 is one individual, not a population: a boy who died in infancy. His bones are dated to 12,707–12,556 years ago and were found directly associated with Clovis tools, so his DNA is tied to that archaeological tradition through the burial itself. His genome was sequenced to 14.4-fold coverage, meaning that on average each position in it was read more than 14 times.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Within the Americas, his closest relatives live to the south. Compared with 52 present-day Native American groups, his genome shares less history with seven northern groups than with 44 in Central and South America, and it is compatible with his belonging to a population directly ancestral to the present-day Karitiana and Maya. He carries the Mal'ta-related ancestry, named after a 24,000-year-old Siberian individual, that entered the ancestors of Native Americans, so that mixing had already happened by his lifetime. The analysis places him on or near the southern Native American lineage, which means the northern and southern lineages had already separated.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Ancestry with a particular affinity to Anzick-1 turns up far to the south. Posth and colleagues (2018) find it highest among South Americans in the oldest individuals, from Los Rieles in Chile about 10,900 years ago and Lapa do Santo in Brazil about 9,600 years ago, and in later individuals from the Central Andes. They see in it one of two streams of ancestry from north to south, linking him to the oldest individuals from Chile, Brazil and Belize. Later South Americans derive from lineages without this specific Clovis affinity, which the authors explain as a population replacement that began at least 9,000 years ago and was followed by long regional continuity.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: What the southern link means is open. Posth and colleagues say their data fit two different histories: nearly all South American ancestry may have come from movements out of North America after Clovis times, or a different ancestry, unrelated to Anzick-1, may have moved south earlier, before Clovis, such as at Monte Verde. The Belize part of the link is also weak: the oldest Belize individual shows only slight evidence of more relatedness to Anzick-1 than later Belize individuals do.

caveats: This page describes a single individual; he does not stand for everyone who made or used Clovis tools.

early-central-south-americans.description: The earliest people of Central and South America whose genomes have been read, who lived from Belize to Chile more than 8,000 years ago. Their DNA records a rapid spread into many lineages at once, and they share little specific ancestry with present-day people.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The core evidence is a 2018 study by Posth and colleagues that followed four regions through time: Belize, Brazil, the Central Andes and the Southern Cone at the continent's southern end. Its 49 individuals form four time series, each beginning between 10,900 and 8,600 years ago, so later changes can be measured against the earliest people of the same region. Among the oldest are remains from Los Rieles in Chile, about 10,900 years old, from Lapa do Santo in Brazil, about 9,600 years old, and from Belize, about 9,300 years old.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Their genomes record a fast spread. Nine ancient groups fit a star-shaped family tree branching from a single source population, which sits on one of the two early Native American branches. The five earliest lineages, in Belize, Peru, the Southern Cone, Lapa do Santo and Los Rieles, split so close together in time that their order cannot be worked out. The authors read this as a rapid radiation of the main lineage ancestral to later South Americans.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Some of the earliest individuals carry a link to North America that later South Americans lack. The people at Los Rieles and Lapa do Santo share more genetic variants with Anzick-1, the infant buried with Clovis tools in Montana, than other South Americans do, except later individuals from the Central Andes. The authors see in this one of two streams of ancestry from north to south. Later South Americans derive from lineages without that Clovis-linked affinity, which the authors explain as a population replacement beginning at least 9,000 years ago, followed by long continuity within each region.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Two questions stay open. One is what the Anzick-1 link means: Posth and colleagues say their data fit either an early, pre-Clovis spread of a different ancestry, such as at Monte Verde, or nearly all South American ancestry coming from movements out of North America after Clovis. The other is an Australasian-related signal that Skoglund and colleagues reported in some present-day Amazonian groups, such as the Surui. No ancient Central or South American tested by Posth and colleagues shows it, including Lapa do Santo individuals whose skulls have the shape called 'Paleoamerican', though a second 2018 study, checked only in its abstract, reports one early migration that carried such a signal.

caveats: The page groups individuals from Central and South America dated before about 8,000 years ago by region and date; they do not form one genetic cluster.
AADR labels for early Belize individuals contain 'Archaic_Maya', projecting a much later identity back in time; we keep the label as data only.

central-andes.description: Ancient individuals of the Andean highlands and coast, whose genomes show the regional differences seen today beginning to form by about 5,800 years ago. From about 2,000 years ago, most regions stayed genetically uniform even as archaeological cultures changed.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This is a region followed across about 8,500 years, not a single population. Its core is a 2020 study by Nakatsuka and colleagues of 89 individuals from the Central and South-Central Andes, 65 of them newly reported, who lived between about 9,000 and 500 years ago. They come from highland and coastal contexts associated with the Wari, Tiwanaku, Moche and Inca cultures, among others.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The pattern of genetic differences between Andean regions seen today began to form by about 5,800 years ago. The study infers that by then the northern and southern highland lineages had already split, and that even the oldest highland individuals, from Lauricocha about 8,600 years ago, were distinct from coastal groups. Gene flow nonetheless linked the north and south highlands, and the highlands and the coast. Posth and colleagues (2018) suggest that the oldest Peruvian individuals, from Cuncaicha and Lauricocha and up to about 9,000 years old, share genetic variants at the highest rate with present-day Indigenous groups of the Central Andes.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Posth and colleagues also report a stream of gene flow with a distinctive affinity to individuals from San Nicolas Island, California, who lived about 4,900 years ago; it was present in the Central Andes by about 4,200 years ago. After about 2,000 years ago most regions stayed genetically uniform through changes of archaeological culture, including the shift from Moche to Lambayeque and Wari influence, and neighbouring groups show minimal mixing between 2,000 and 500 years ago. The exceptions are the Tiwanaku and Inca heartlands, where communities were of mixed ancestry, and the study points to long-range mobility and genetic heterogeneity at Tiwanaku and, in the Inca period, in the Cusco and Sacred Valley regions. Present-day Indigenous groups cluster with ancient individuals from their own region.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The match between ancient and present-day groups is not universal: pre-Hispanic Cusco individuals are less closely related to present-day Cusco individuals than to groups outside the region, and the study offers several possible explanations. Where the match does hold, the authors stress that it shows genetic continuity only, not continuity of language. The age given for the split between the northern and southern highland lineages is only a lower limit, so when it happened is open.

caveats: The page groups individuals from Peru and Bolivia by region, not by a shared genetic profile; because the regions differ genetically, no single average describes them.

caribbean-archaic.description: People of the Caribbean's Archaic Age, before the Ceramic Age, whose DNA is closest to that of Central and northern South Americans. Their lineages were later more than 98 percent replaced by a ceramic-using population, yet in western Cuba they persisted for over 2,500 years.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The study's Greater Antilles Archaic clade, a branch of the genetic family tree, is almost entirely Cuban: it holds 50 Cuban individuals dated about 3,200 to 700 years ago and one Dominican individual. The Caribbean was first settled about 6,000 years ago, so even the oldest of these individuals lived some 2,800 years after the first settlement. Their communities appear to have been small: effective population size, a genetic estimate of how many individuals contributed to the next generation, is put at about 200–300 at Archaic-associated sites, against 500–1,500 at Ceramic-associated ones.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The study traces the Archaic Age people to a deeply divergent population, meaning a lineage with a long history apart from its relatives. Their genomes share the most genetic history with Indigenous groups from Central and northern South America, and show no excess sharing with Mesoamerican or North American groups. The study found no support for earlier claims of North American-related ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The Caribbean shifted from the Archaic to the Ceramic Age around 2,500 years ago. Archaic lineages were more than 98 percent replaced by a homogeneous ceramic-using population, which the study relates to northeastern South America and which reached the Greater Antilles at least 1,700 years ago. Western Cuba is the exception: there, Archaic lineages persisted with minimal mixture for more than 2,500 years.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The evidence shows who the Archaic Age people were most closely related to, not where their ancestors lived before reaching the islands. Because all but one of the individuals in the clade are Cuban, the findings speak mainly for Cuba. Why Archaic lineages persisted in western Cuba when they gave way elsewhere is not explained by this evidence.

caribbean-ceramic.description: The ceramic-using people who spread through the Caribbean islands, carrying almost none of the ancestry of the Archaic Age people before them. Their genomes show one homogeneous, interconnected population, though its link to Arawak-speaking groups of northeastern South America depends on the method used.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The group is defined by archaeology: individuals associated with the Ceramic Age. The 2021 study by Fernandes and colleagues analysed 194 of them, dated about 1,700 to 400 years ago, and finds them genetically homogeneous. They were not isolated island by island: 19 pairs of cross-island cousins show an interconnected population, with an estimated effective population size of about 500–1,500, a genetic measure of how many individuals contributed to each next generation.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Almost none of the Archaic Age people's ancestry survives in them: Archaic-related ancestry in ceramic-associated people of the Greater Antilles and The Bahamas is estimated at about 0.5–2.0 percent, with the exception of three individuals in Hispaniola, who carry 11.8–18.5 percent. The rest of their ancestry fits a source population related to groups of northeastern South America. Models in which the Lesser Antilles supplied the ancestry of the Greater Antillean groups fit the data, which points to a spread from south to north.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The ceramic-using population followed the Archaic Age people: the Caribbean shifted from the Archaic to the Ceramic Age around 2,500 years ago, and the population reached the Greater Antilles at least 1,700 years ago. Within the Ceramic Age, changes in pottery style were not driven by migrations of genetically distinct groups. Present-day Puerto Ricans show relatedness to ceramic-associated individuals in two datasets, consistent with Indigenous ancestry that is entirely Ceramic-related but not entirely Archaic-related, an inference drawn from modern genomes.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The study's own analyses diverge on where the expansion came from. The abstract relates the ceramic-using population to Arawak speakers of northeastern South America and an ADMIXTURE analysis suggests the same affinity, but f4 statistics, which compare how much history groups share, find no significant closeness to Arawak-speaking groups over Cariban- or Tupian-speaking ones. These language names label the comparison groups, not the ancient people. Ancient Venezuelans from Las Locas, about 2,350 years old, form a single branch with present-day Cabecar, which the authors read as pointing to more easterly origins. The study found no genetic evidence for a separate Carib migration about 1,150 years ago, though it could not have detected such ancestry below about 2–8 percent.

support.text: The ceramic-using people who spread through the Caribbean islands, carrying almost none of the ancestry of the Archaic Age people before them.
Their genomes show one homogeneous, interconnected population, though its link to Arawak-speaking groups of northeastern South America depends on the method used.
The group is defined by archaeology: individuals associated with the Ceramic Age.
The 2021 study by Fernandes and colleagues analysed 194 of them, dated about 1,700 to 400 years ago, and finds them genetically homogeneous.

They were not isolated island by island: 19 pairs of cross-island cousins show an interconnected population, with an estimated effective population size of about 500–1,500, a genetic measure of how many individuals contributed to each next generation.

Almost none of the Archaic Age people's ancestry survives in them: Archaic-related ancestry in ceramic-associated people of the Greater Antilles and The Bahamas is estimated at about 0.5–2.0 percent, with the exception of three individuals in Hispaniola, who carry 11.8–18.5 percent.
The rest of their ancestry fits a source population related to groups of northeastern South America.
Models in which the Lesser Antilles supplied the ancestry of the Greater Antillean groups fit the data, which points to a spread from south to north.

The ceramic-using population followed the Archaic Age people: the Caribbean shifted from the Archaic to the Ceramic Age around 2,500 years ago, and the population reached the Greater Antilles at least 1,700 years ago.
Within the Ceramic Age, changes in pottery style were not driven by migrations of genetically distinct groups.

Present-day Puerto Ricans show relatedness to ceramic-associated individuals in two datasets, consistent with Indigenous ancestry that is entirely Ceramic-related but not entirely Archaic-related, an inference drawn from modern genomes.
The study's own analyses diverge on where the expansion came from.

The abstract relates the ceramic-using population to Arawak speakers of northeastern South America and an ADMIXTURE analysis suggests the same affinity, but f4 statistics, which compare how much history groups share, find no significant closeness to Arawak-speaking groups over Cariban- or Tupian-speaking ones.
These language names label the comparison groups, not the ancient people.

wanted: first-americans-founders: who the Athabascans and Amerindians of Raghavan et al. 2015 are (a one-clause gloss), so the lower-latitude split reads clearly.

first-americans-founders: a full-text check of the Moreno-Mayar et al. 2018 demographic model (all its dates are abstract-only), and whether Raghavan 2015's 'two basal branches' are the same northern and southern branches it dates, so the two estimates can be compared directly.

ancient-beringians: what USR1 was (an infant, and how it was found at Upward Sun River) and what is known of the second Upward Sun River individual on the map (USR2); no evidence statement describes either, so the page cannot say 'infant' or 'burial'.

clovis-anzick: an evidence statement on the burial context (the old text mentioned red ochre and called it the only known Clovis burial; no evidence carries either) and one defining the Solutrean hypothesis, which the text glosses only as 'the idea that Clovis toolmaking came from Europe'.
clovis-anzick / early-central-south-americans: where and what Monte Verde is, and its date, so the pre-Clovis alternative can be explained rather than just named.

early-central-south-americans: which individual carries the Australasian-related signal in Moreno-Mayar et al. 2018b (full text), so the disagreement with Posth et al. 2018 can be stated site by site; several Lagoa Santa (Sumidouro) individuals from that study are on the map.

central-andes: how many of the oldest highland individuals are sampled and whether Nakatsuka et al. 2020 could determine the direction of gene flow between the North and South Highlands (the old text said it could not; no evidence statement says so).
central-andes: the several possible explanations Nakatsuka et al. 2020 give for why pre-Hispanic Cusco individuals are less related to present-day Cusco individuals than to groups outside the region.
central-andes: dates and places for the Wari, Tiwanaku, Moche, Lambayeque and Inca contexts, so the changes of archaeological culture can be placed on the timeline.

caribbean-archaic / caribbean-ceramic: an evidence statement saying how the Archaic-to-Ceramic Age shift (around 2,500 years ago) relates to the arrival of the ceramic-using population in the Greater Antilles (at least 1,700 years ago), and whether the Archaic Age began with the first settlement about 6,000 years ago; the sampled Archaic individuals are dated 3,200 to 700 years ago.

caribbean-archaic: where in western Cuba the persisting Archaic lineages were sampled, and the sample counts for the islands other than Cuba (the map has three Dominican Republic pre-ceramic individuals, the cited clade statement counts one).

caribbean-ceramic: which islands the 194 Ceramic Age individuals come from (ev-fernandes2021-am4 gives only the total and dates), and what the Las Locas result's 'more easterly origins' is relative to; a full-text statement would let the Venezuelan coast be placed.
caribbean-ceramic: who the Carib migration of about 1,150 years ago refers to in the paper (one clause), so the 2–8 percent detection limit can be explained.
concerns: ancient-beringians: ev-raghavan2015-am1 is linked to this population, but it concerns the later split between Athabascan and Amerindian lineages, not the Ancient Beringian split; the old text presented it as a competing location for the Ancient Beringian split. The new text states what it is about.

ancient-beringians: the old caveat said all claims were verified against the abstract only, but ev-posth2018-am1 and both Sikora 2019 statements are full-text; the caveat has been narrowed to the Moreno-Mayar 2018 claims.
clovis-anzick: the old 'Who they were' stated red ochre in the burial and that Anzick-1 is the only known Clovis burial; neither is in any evidence statement (removed).

clovis-anzick: the map dates Anzick-1 to 10797–10726 calBCE (AADR), while Rasmussen et al. 2014 (ev-rasmussen2014-am2) give 12,707–12,556 cal BP, about 10,758–10,607 BCE; the two ranges barely overlap and the source of the difference should be checked.

clovis-anzick / early-central-south-americans / central-andes: ev-posth2018-am2 says later Central Andes individuals share more Anzick-1 relatedness than other South Americans, while ev-posth2018-4 says later South Americans derive from lineages without specific Clovis affinity; both are quoted faithfully, but the paper should be checked for how they fit together (possibly via the ~4,200-year-old stream).

early-central-south-americans: evidence gives Los Rieles as about 10,900 years old (ev-posth2018-am2, -am3), but the AADR date on the map for I11974 (label Chile_LosRieles_12000BP) is 10420–9450 calBCE, roughly 12,400–11,400 years ago; one of the two needs checking.

early-central-south-americans / central-andes: Lauricocha individual I0238 (7000–6000 BCE) is a member of both populations because its date range straddles the 8,000-year boundary; and several map individuals come from studies with no curated source or evidence (Kennett et al. 2022 Belize incl. an 11,700 BP label, Ferraz et al. 2023, Maravall-López et al. 2025).

caribbean-archaic / caribbean-ceramic: ev-fernandes2021-am3 (shift to the Ceramic Age around 2,500 years ago) and ev-fernandes2021-3 (ceramic-using population reached the Greater Antilles at least 1,700 years ago) give different dates for what reads as one event; the paper should be checked for how they fit together.
